sentence: It meets your skin's outer layer, which bends light about as strongly as glass.
claim: The refractive index of dry stratum corneum is about 1.55 (reported values range about 1.45–1.55; 1.53–1.54 also appear), against 1.0 for air.
source_title: Journal of the Society of Cosmetic Chemists 28(3), 1977: light transmission through stratum corneum in immersion liquids
note: Excerpt: transmission 'peak at 1.54 is very close to the index of refraction of human stratum corneum'; 'human skin is reported to have an index of refraction number of 1.55'. Cross-checks: an OCT paper uses 'n = 1.55 of the stratum corneum'; a patent: 'air (ηD=1.0) and dry stratum corneum (ηD=1.55)'; a confocal-imaging paper (arXiv physics/0401104) lists 1.53. Screen shows '≈ 1.55'.

sentence: It meets your skin's outer layer, which bends light about as strongly as glass.
claim: Ordinary glass has a refractive index of about 1.5, reflecting about 4% of light at each surface at normal incidence.
source_title: Fresnel equations (Wikipedia); worked example: Kiel University materials-science exercise 5.2.1
note: Excerpts: 'about 4% for common glass' in air (per surface); Kiel exercise: n = 1.5 gives (0.5/2.5)² = 0.04. Stratum corneum 1.55 vs glass 1.5: 'about as strongly as glass'. Secondary source for a physics fact; swap for a textbook if the reviewer prefers.

sentence: So only a few percent bounces straight back off the top, as a glint.
claim: Only about 4–7% of light striking skin near head-on is reflected at the surface (regular/specular reflection at the air–stratum corneum boundary), across 250–3000 nm.
source_title: Lister T, Wright PA, Chappell PH. Optical properties of human skin. J Biomed Opt 2012;17(9):090901
note: Excerpt (Lister 2012, cut off in the snippet): 'it has been estimated that 4% to 7% of visible light' [is reflected at the surface]. Cross-checks: patents citing Scheuplein, J Soc Cosmet Chem 1964;15:111–122: 'specular reflectance of a nearly perpendicular beam from normal skin is always between 4–7% over the entire spectrum from 250–3000 nm'; S. Jacques (omlc.org): about 5% 'reflected from the surface as glare'. Fresnel with n 1.55 gives ≈ 4.7% (computed). Said 'a few percent'.

sentence: Smooth and full of water, that layer sends the glint back in one clean direction, like a mirror.
claim: Hydrating the stratum corneum makes skin measurably smoother (and the stratum corneum thicker), with the fastest water uptake in the upper few micrometres.
source_title: Dąbrowska AK et al. In vivo confirmation of hydration-induced changes in human-skin thickness, roughness and interaction with the environment. Biointerphases 2016;11(3):031015
note: Excerpt: 'Hydrated skin was smoother and exhibited higher real contact area values'; 'highest rates of water uptake were observed for the upper few micrometers of skin'. Caveat: a single-participant pilot study (volar forearm); badged 'one study'.

sentence: Smooth and full of water, that layer sends the glint back in one clean direction, like a mirror.
claim: A smoother surface reflects light more specularly (in one direction, mirror-like); skin's perceived gloss falls as its microscale roughness rises.
source_title: Journal of Perceptual Imaging (IS&T): perceived facial gloss vs microscale skin roughness in rendered faces
note: Excerpt: 'an exponential relationship between microscale skin roughness and perceived facial gloss', consistent across skin tones. Cross-check (IS&T Electronic Imaging 2017): more surface-reflection contrast raised perceived gloss. Physics of specular vs diffuse reflection is textbook; the 'mirror' is the image for specular.

sentence: Dry it out, and it scatters light every which way.
claim: When skin is dehydrated, its surface (stratum corneum) scatters more light; hydration lowers that scattering and makes skin more translucent.
source_title: Jiang Z-X, DeLaCruz J. Appearance benefits of skin moisturization. Skin Res Technol 2011;17(1):51–55
note: Excerpt: 'Both spectral reflectance and scattering coefficient increased when skin was dehydrated and decreased when it was hydrated. Translucency increased as the skin became moisturized.' Authors hypothesised 'the major optical effect of skin moisturization is the decrease of light scattering at the skin surface, i.e., the stratum corneum.' Industry authors; badged 'one study'.

sentence: But it's the small part: most light slips inside, bounces among cells and fibres, and a large share comes back out.
claim: Since only about 4–7% is reflected at the surface, the great majority of light striking skin (about 93–96%) enters it.
source_title: Lister T, Wright PA, Chappell PH. Optical properties of human skin. J Biomed Opt 2012;17(9):090901
note: Computed from c3's 4–7%: 100 − (4 to 7) = 93–96%. Press cross-check (Bangkok Post): '4% to 7% ... reflected on the skin's surface, and more than 90% penetrates the skin'. Said 'most light slips inside'.

sentence: But it's the small part: most light slips inside, bounces among cells and fibres, and a large share comes back out.
claim: Light inside skin is scattered many times by cells and fibres; in one worked example about 40% of incident light is backscattered out of the skin after multiple scattering, against about 5% surface glare (the rest, about 53%, absorbed).
source_title: Jacques SL. Skin optics / polarized-light imaging notes (Oregon Medical Laser Center, 1999)
note: Excerpt: about 5% 'reflected from the surface as glare'; about 2% from superficial layers; 'about 40% penetrates deeply and is backscattered to the surface after multiple scatterings'; about 53% absorbed. One example (a specific wavelength and set-up), badged 'one example (model)'. Said 'a large share'. Lister 2012: collagen fibres dominate dermal scattering.

sentence: Melanin and blood tint it on the way, and a rush of blood sends it back redder.
claim: Melanin (in the epidermis) and haemoglobin in blood (in the dermis) are the main absorbers of visible light in skin, and so colour the light that comes back out.
source_title: Lister T, Wright PA, Chappell PH. Optical properties of human skin. J Biomed Opt 2012;17(9):090901
note: Excerpt: haemoglobin and melanin named as the two main visible-light absorbers; 'hemoglobin dominates absorption in the dermis', melanin in the epidermis. Cross-check (Hunter, J Soc Cosmet Chem): 'Haemoglobin, oxyhaemoglobin, melanin and carotene are pigments responsible for the colour of human skin'; pink of light skin from haemoglobin in superficial dermal vessels.

sentence: Melanin and blood tint it on the way, and a rush of blood sends it back redder.
claim: Flushing occurs because the blood vessels in the skin dilate; more blood near the surface makes the skin look redder.
note: Excerpt: 'Flushing occurs because the blood vessels in the skin dilate.' Secondary: 'blood vessels in the skin dilate, increasing blood flow to the surface. This increased blood flow causes the skin to appear red.' Search returned the older URL dermnetnz.org/vascular/flushing.html. Said 'a rush of blood'; no condition named.

sentence: Asked to make a face look healthy, people turned that up.
claim: When people adjusted colour-calibrated face photos to look as healthy as possible, they increased skin blood colour, particularly oxygenated blood colour, above baseline.
source_title: Stephen ID, Coetzee V, Law Smith M, Perrett DI. Skin blood perfusion and oxygenation colour affect perceived human health. PLoS ONE 2009;4(4):e5083
note: Excerpt: 'Participants increased skin blood colour, particularly oxygenated, above basal levels to optimise healthy appearance.' Perceived health only, not actual health; on screen with a model face.

sentence: Blue light gets barely a millimetre in, about ten sheets of paper; red light goes several times deeper.
claim: In skin, blue light barely penetrates about 1 mm, whereas red light is extinguished some 4–5 mm beneath the surface; penetration increases with wavelength.
source_title: Ash C, Dubec M, Donne K, Bashford T. Effect of wavelength and beam width on penetration in light-tissue interaction using computational methods. Lasers Med Sci 2017;32(8):1909–1918 (PMC5653719)
note: Excerpt: 'red light is extinguished some 4–5 mm beneath the surface of the skin whereas ultraviolet hardly penetrates at all and blue barely 1 mm into tissue'; abstract: penetration depth increases with wavelength. Depths vary with skin, site and beam (iScience review table, after Bashkatov 2005: ≈ 0.3–2 mm across 400–700 nm). 'Several times deeper' = 4–5× (computed).

sentence: Blue light gets barely a millimetre in, about ten sheets of paper; red light goes several times deeper.
claim: A sheet of ordinary 80 gsm copy paper is about 100 µm thick.
source_title: Papers and boards: category and standards (WJEC, UK education resource)
note: As Outer Layer No. 001's paper claim (its source). Computed: 1 mm ÷ 100 µm = 10 sheets.

sentence: Blue light gets barely a millimetre in, about ten sheets of paper; red light goes several times deeper.
claim: Red light (about 625–700 nm) can reach through the full thickness of the skin, while blue light stays near the surface.
source_title: PMC review (PMC8887026) on light wavelengths and skin penetration
note: Excerpt: blue light 'is higher energy than red light but has less penetration'; red light 'can penetrate the full skin thickness'. Cross-check: 2020 Monte Carlo study (Spectroscopy and Spectral Analysis 40(4)): blue reaches only the surface layer, red reaches the dermis.

sentence: Mostly from within: light that went in, met your blood, and came back.
claim: Of the light coming back from skin, much more has travelled inside it and been scattered back out (about 40% of incident light in one example) than is reflected at the surface (about 4–7%); that returning light carries the colour of melanin and blood.
source_title: Jacques SL. Skin optics / polarized-light imaging notes (Oregon Medical Laser Center, 1999)
note: As c8 (≈ 40% backscattered after multiple scattering vs ≈ 5% glare) and c9 (melanin, haemoglobin). 'Mostly from within' rests on that one example; the ratio changes with wavelength and skin tone (more melanin absorbs more), so the reviewer should confirm the wording holds for deeply pigmented skin.
